prompt.context: As an established consultant with McKinsey, you have volunteered your time to critique business plans at a local entrepreneur's forum. One plan calls for establishing door-to-door distribution of an already existing online newspaper in Cologne, the fourth-largest city in Germany.
prompt.question: Without detailed knowledge of how the process would work in practice, how might you evaluate the feasibility of the proposed distribution plan?

clarifying_info.q: What resources are available for distribution?
clarifying_info.a: No external capital has been provided. Resources only allow for the hiring of 6 newspaper carriers on bicycles, each responsible for one square kilometer within the downtown area.

clarifying_info.q: What shape should we assume for the city, and how is the population distributed?
clarifying_info.a: Assume the city is in the shape of a square and the population is evenly distributed in homes that are an equal distance apart from each other. Ignore non-residential areas and assume no stacking of homes.

clarifying_info.q: What are the delivery time constraints?
clarifying_info.a: The newspaper is printed and ready for distribution by 4AM each morning and must be delivered by 6AM to meet customer requirements.

clarifying_info.q: How far apart are subscriber homes on average?
clarifying_info.a: Assume subscriber homes within the proposed distribution area are on average 10 meters apart from each other.

exhibits.title: Grid of subscriber homes in one square kilometer
exhibits.shows: A dot-grid diagram illustrating the layout of subscriber homes spaced evenly across a square area, with dots arranged in rows and columns extending to 100 homes per side
exhibits.data: Grid rows of dots representing homes; label '100' at far end of bottom row indicating 100 homes per side of the square kilometer

framework: Define the feasibility question: can newspaper carriers physically complete delivery within the allotted time window?
Quantify the delivery area: determine number of homes (stops) per square kilometer given the spacing assumption
Quantify available time: calculate total seconds in the 2-hour delivery window (4AM–6AM)
Calculate required pace: divide number of stops by available seconds to get seconds-per-delivery
Evaluate reasonableness: assess whether the required pace is physically achievable
Identify solutions if infeasible: propose alternatives to make the plan viable

questions.prompt: How many subscriber homes (stops) does each carrier need to service within their 1 square kilometer area?
questions.guidance: The candidate should use the 10-meter spacing assumption. A 1 km = 1,000 m side divided by 10 m between homes gives 100 homes per side. A square kilometer therefore contains 100 x 100 = 10,000 stops per carrier.

math.setup: 1 km = 1,000 m; homes are 10 m apart; area is a square
steps: Homes per side = 1,000 m / 10 m = 100 homes
Stops per sq km = 100 homes/row × 100 rows = 10,000 stops
math.answer: 10,000 stops per carrier per square kilometer

questions.prompt: How many seconds does each carrier have to complete delivery of their area?
questions.guidance: The window is 4AM to 6AM, exactly 2 hours. The candidate should convert this to seconds.

questions.prompt: Given the number of stops and the available time, how quickly must each delivery be made? Is this feasible?
questions.guidance: Divide available seconds by number of stops to get time per delivery. The result is less than 1 second per stop, which is not physically achievable on a bicycle — the carrier must deliver more than one newspaper per second.

math.setup: Time per stop = total seconds / total stops
steps: Equivalently: more than 1 newspaper must be delivered per second
math.answer: 0.72 seconds per stop — more than 1 delivery per second, which is physically impossible

brainstorming.prompt: Given the plan is infeasible as structured, what solutions could make it viable?

categories.name: Reduce distribution area
ideas: Pare back the coverage zone to only the most profitable or densely subscribed neighborhoods
Focus on a smaller radius where subscriber density is highest, reducing total stops
Use subscriber data to identify highest-value clusters and limit delivery to those blocks

categories.name: Change distribution method
ideas: Co-distribute with other publications to share costs and allow hiring of more carriers
Use alternative channels such as newspaper stands, kiosks, or pick-up points instead of door-to-door
Partner with existing delivery networks (e.g., postal service or couriers) that already have infrastructure
Shift to a motorized delivery vehicle instead of bicycles to increase speed

recommendation: The proposed door-to-door distribution plan is not feasible as currently designed: with 6 carriers each covering 1 sq km, each carrier would need to deliver one newspaper every 0.72 seconds over 2 hours, which is physically impossible
The business plan must either reduce the distribution footprint or fundamentally change the delivery method before launch
risks: If distribution area is reduced, subscriber reach and revenue potential also shrink, potentially threatening the business model
Co-distribution arrangements may involve complex negotiations and revenue sharing that erode margins
next_steps: Model the minimum viable subscriber density and area that allows feasible delivery within constraints
Evaluate co-distribution partnerships with established local publications
Assess cost-benefit of motorized carriers vs. bicycle carriers to expand coverage without adding headcount
